definition: When adapting an existing, previously-established character into a new game or genre, judge the result against two SEPARATE, independently-gradable goals rather than one blended impression: whether the character aesthetically still feels like themselves (proportions, attitude, iconic silhouette and signature moves preserved) and whether their moveset functionally handles like the new genre demands (speed, clarity, responsiveness) — and note that a character can fully succeed on BOTH of those while still having a third, separate gap: whether the moveset's own CONTENT (which abilities exist at all) actually foregrounds what is most identity-defining about the character, independent of how well any single move is posed or timed.
purpose: Give a reviewer or director a structured way to diagnose WHERE an adaptation is falling short, since a weak result on each axis needs a completely different fix — re-posing/re-timing for the functional axis, redesigning silhouette or references for the aesthetic axis, or reconsidering which abilities exist at all for the moveset-content axis — and conflating the three risks fixing the wrong one.
visible_effect: Three structurally different kinds of departure from 'this adaptation feels right' are possible independently: wrong proportions/attitude/silhouette reads as 'doesn't look like the character'; wrong speed/clarity reads as 'doesn't play right for this genre'; and — even with both of those fully correct — a moveset that underuses the character's own signature trait reads as a specific, separate missed-opportunity feeling neither of the other two axes explains.
psychological_or_gameplay_effect: The source's own worked example: Mario's Smash Bros. moveset is judged a full success on both the aesthetic axis (proportions, attitude, silhouette, direct references to Mario 64's own combo and throw all preserved) and the functional axis (speed, clarity, hit-feedback all genre-appropriate), yet the same source still identifies a real gap — jumping, Mario's single most identity-defining trait, plays almost no role in his moveset's actual content, unlike either failure the first two axes would predict.
physical_interpretation: None — a review/direction framework, not a physical property.
use_cases: adapting any pre-established character (from another game, medium, or an earlier installment of the same franchise) into a new genre or engine, where both 'does it still look like them' and 'does it play right here' need separate, explicit answers
diagnosing a lukewarm reception to an adaptation that nobody can pin down — checking each axis separately (and the moveset-content axis specifically) narrows down which one is actually failing
non_use_cases: designing a wholly original character with no prior identity to preserve, where the aesthetic-fidelity axis has no external reference to be measured against

a single isolated shot or move review, where Cadence's own existing quality hierarchy (Part 14, `ai/review.js`) already applies and this broader, whole-character adaptation framework is not the relevant scale
interactions: matching_own_fidelity_down_to_source_material_budget (video 52, this same batch) — a specific instance of this entry's AESTHETIC axis: matching a source's own established fidelity convention is one concrete way to satisfy 'still feels like the character'

handedness_swap_for_camera_facing_pose_openness (video 53, this same video) — a concrete technique serving this entry's FUNCTIONAL axis (genre-appropriate readability), demonstrated on the very same worked example

Part 14's quality hierarchy (`ai/review.js QUALITY_LAYERS`) — layer 1 ('intent and purpose') is the closest existing analogue to this entry's functional axis, but is scoped to whether a shot serves ITS OWN declared `AcceptanceSpec`, not to whether a moveset's content faithfully represents a pre-existing external character's identity; this entry's aesthetic-fidelity and moveset-content axes sit entirely outside all thirteen existing layers
cadence_representation: Not represented as a distinct review axis. `ai/review.js`'s Part 14 quality hierarchy has thirteen layers ordered for judging ONE shot's own internal consistency (readability, pose design, timing, spacing, weight, contacts, arcs, overlap, camera, VFX, secondary motion, polish) — layer 1, 'intent and purpose', is the only one that references a declared goal at all, and even that is scoped to whatever `AcceptanceSpec` the shot itself supplies, not to fidelity against a pre-existing external character's own established identity. This entry names a genuinely different, adaptation-specific axis that sits above and outside all thirteen existing layers: nothing in this build asks 'does this whole character's moveset content still centre on what made them recognisable in the first place.'
control_surface: None — no tool declares or checks a moveset's aggregate identity-fidelity against an external reference character.
detection_and_measurement_methods: Not measurable in this build: this is a whole-character, whole-moveset judgment against an external reference identity, not a property any single clip's motion data could reveal. `ai/reference.js`'s Part 36 profile/distance tooling could in principle compare individual MOTION characteristics against an imported reference clip (as noted in `matching_own_fidelity_down_to_source_material_budget`), but nothing evaluates moveset CONTENT — which abilities exist at all — against a character's own established identity.
failure_modes: fixing the wrong axis: re-timing an attack that is already functionally fine when the real complaint is aesthetic (or vice versa)

assuming aesthetic and functional success together mean the adaptation is complete — the source's own worked example shows a character can pass both while still under-using their single most identity-defining trait in the moveset's own CONTENT

judging aesthetic fidelity only against a character's most recent appearance, when a character's identity may be better served by an earlier, more distinctive convention (this same batch's video 52 finding, `matching_own_fidelity_down_to_source_material_budget`)
roblox_considerations: Directly applicable to any Roblox project adapting a licensed or previously-established character/IP into a new experience — the same three-axis diagnostic (looks like them / plays right for this genre / moveset content reflects their identity) applies regardless of engine.
examples: 'those are the two parallel animation goals for adapting any character to Smash Brothers: they must aesthetically feel like the character you know and love, while also functionally handling like a Smash Brothers character' (video @ 04:22–04:37)

the source's own verdict, both axes satisfied: 'does the Smash Brothers incarnation of Mario feel like Mario? I would say yes... his moveset is packed with references to previous Mario games... [and] this is some darned good game animation right here, functionality and aesthetics both firing on all cylinders' (video @ 06:31–09:22)

the third, separate gap the source identifies despite both axes succeeding: 'I am still really surprised at how little jumping plays into Mario's moveset... there's a big opportunity being missed to capitalize on something that makes Mario's mobility and combat style feel really unique' (video @ 09:58–10:23)
